title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbooks — Standards
author: Ari Chen
content:
Summary

This document defines Redwood Inference’s SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs), error budget policy, capacity planning process, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and runbook templates. It is intended for service owners, on-call SREs, and product engineers who operate production endpoints (hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private deployments).

Scope

- Applies to all externally customer-facing inference endpoints and internal critical control plane services.
- Does not replace per-service SLOs; this page defines the company-wide standard and templates for teams to adopt.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Principles
- SLOs must reflect user experience and business impact (latency, availability, correctness).
- Keep SLOs simple and measurable with high signal-to-noise metrics.
- One latency or correctness SLO + one availability SLO is the recommended minimum for every service.

Required SLOs
- Availability SLO (synthetic + production traffic): target >= 99.95% monthly for user-facing inference routes by default. Exceptions require documented approval and compensating controls.
- Latency SLOs for generation endpoints: p95 <= 200ms for routing/metadata ops; for text generation p95 <= 800ms for short sequences (<=128 tokens). Teams serving longer sequences must define sequence-length buckets (e.g., <=128, 129–512, >512) with explicit SLOs.
- Correctness/Quality SLOs (optional where applicable): e.g., embedding similarity regression thresholds, prompt-set eval pass rate >= 98%.

SLO Table (template)
| SLO name | Metric | Window | Target | Measurement source | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Inference availability | successful requests / total requests (5xx and 429 considered failures) | 30d rolling | 99.95% | prod-telemetry (service-metrics.prom) | svc-team |
| Short-gen latency p95 | request_latency_ms{route="/v1/generate", seq_len_bucket="<=128"} | 30d rolling | <= 800ms | observability/tempo + metrics | svc-team |
| Control plane RPC success | rpc_success_ratio | 30d rolling | 99.9% | controlplane-metrics | infra-team |

Notes:
- Failure definition: HTTP 5xx and 429 are failures; 4xx from client input are not. For private deployments, failures also include known model OOMs and kernel panics captured by the runtime.

2) Measurement and Instrumentation

- Use central metrics pipeline: emit metrics with consistent labels (service, route, cluster, model_family, seq_len_bucket, customer_tier).
- Instrumentations required: request_id tracing, latency histogram (p50/p95/p99), request size, token count, error type (5xx/429/model_error), and backend host.
- Synthetic checks: run global synthetic probes (US, EU, APAC) for critical routes every 60s; synthetic failures count towards availability SLO with a weighting factor defined per service (default 0.5 to avoid duplicate counting with production traffic).

3) Error Budget Policy and Burn Rate

- Error budget = (1 - SLO_target) * window. Track burn-rate on 2h and 30d windows.
- Automatic controls triggered by burn-rate thresholds: 
  1) Burn rate > 1.0 (consuming budget faster than allowed) — notify service owners and reduce non-essential background work (auto-scaling config: reduce pre-warming; routing: shift non-critical route traffic to lower-priority pool).
  2) Burn rate > 4.0 — require immediate on-call review and rollback of recent deploys if applicable; escalate to on-call manager.
  3) Burn rate > 8.0 — open a SEV incident and initiate incident playbook.

- Error budget governance:
  - If a service exhausts its monthly error budget, the owner must present a remediation plan within 72 hours and schedule a reliability initiative (see section 5).
  - Product rollouts that increase traffic or change model behavior must allocate error budget and be approved by the SRE liaison.

4) Alerts and Alerting Thresholds

- Alert categories: P0 (SEV), P1 (critical), P2 (warning).
- Minimal alerts for a service:
  - P0: sustained burn rate > 8.0 OR availability < 99.5% for 15m OR p99 latency degrading > 3x baseline for 10m.
  - P1: burn rate between 4 and 8 OR availability < 99.8% for 30m OR p95 latency > SLO target for 30m.
  - P2: single-interval p95 breach OR small synthetic failures.
- Alert routing: SEV alerts page to on-call, with escalation policy (on-call escalation 5m -> secondary 10m -> manager 15m).

5) Capacity Planning

Goals and cadence
- Goal: ensure headroom to meet latency and availability SLOs under P95 traffic and maintain graceful degradation under P99 traffic.
- Quarterly capacity review led by SRE with participation from product and infra teams.

Process
1) Forecast demand using: historical QPS, growth trends, product roadmap events (feature launches), and model changes (larger parameter counts, longer sequences).
2) Convert forecast to GPU/CPU capacity using current throughput profiles per model variant (tokens/sec per GPU, average tokens per request). Use the Capacity Calculator (link in related pages).
3) Define headroom policy: target 30% spare capacity for Hosted API routes, 20% for Dedicated pools; teams can request different targets with justification.
4) Reserve capacity and run load tests for new model variants at +10/20/50% of expected peak.

Capacity runbook checklist (required for quarterly review):
- Traffic and token growth trends (CSV).
- Model catalog and quantization profiles.
- Autoscaling policies and cooldowns.
- Warm pool and pre-warm policies.
- Cost vs latency trade-off analysis.

6) Reliability Initiatives and Postmortem Standards

- Every SEV requires a postmortem within 72 hours containing: timeline, impact, root cause analysis, mitigation steps, action items, and owner for each item. Use the postmortem template.
- Initiatives (root-cause reduction work) should be tracked as JIRA tickets with SLO impact estimates and expected time to complete. Prioritize initiatives that recover the largest error budget or reduce highest-cost incidents.

Postmortem quality rubric (high level)
- Timeline accuracy and evidence: 5/5
- Root cause that identifies systemic fixable failure: 5/5
- Action items with owners and due dates: 5/5
- No-blame language and customer impact clearly described: 5/5

7) Incident Review Standards

- Incident review cadence: weekly SEV review (rotating facilitator) and monthly reliability review with engineering leadership.
- Review must include: detection gap analysis, communication effectiveness, runbook adequacy, monitoring blind spots, and prod-test coverage.
- Celebrate and share learnings: document follow-ups in the reliability initiatives board and update runbooks accordingly.

8) Operational Tooling and Dashboards

Required dashboards
- Service SLO dashboard: SLO compliance, error budget remaining (2h and 30d), burn rate, top error categories.
- Capacity dashboard: cluster utilization, GPU memory pressure, queue length, tail latency by model variant and sequence-length bucket.
- Deployment dashboard: throughput and error delta pre/post-deploy, canary metrics.

Tooling integration requirements
- Metrics: Prometheus-compatible metrics pipeline and OpenTelemetry traces.
- Alerting: PagerDuty for on-call routing and OpsGenie integrations for Dedicated customers where required.
- Runbook storage: canonical runbooks must live in Confluence with a link in the runbook metadata stored in the incidents system.

9) Runbook Templates and Examples

Runbook naming and ownership
- Name: svc-runbook-<service-name>-<primary-sev>. Example: svc-runbook-inference-router-high-cpu.
- Primary owner and secondary owner listed at top with Slack/PagerDuty contacts.

Runbook template sections (required)
- Title, service, owners, pagerduty contact, last tested date.
- Symptoms (what the on-call will see).
- Immediate triage steps (numbered).
- Mitigation steps to restore service (numbered, with exact CLI/HTTP commands).
- Rollback and deployment-safe checks.
- Post-incident follow-up and links to playbooks and postmortem template.

Example runbook: High inference latency (short sequences)
1) Confirm alert and gather context: run: curl -s "https://observability.internal/api/query?service=inference&metric=p95" | jq .
2) Check queue/backlog: kubectl -n inference get pods -o wide; kubectl -n inference logs <pod> | tail -n 200
3) Verify model host health: curl -s http://model-host-01:9000/health || true
4) If pod OOM or model crash: describe pod and increase replica set to a safe number: kubectl scale deployment inference-runtime --replicas=5
5) Temporary mitigation: route <non-critical-customer> traffic to a lower-priority pool: rdctl route set --service inference --pool low-priority --selector non_critical=true
6) If caused by recent deploy: rollback deploy: rdctl rollout undo deployment/inference-runtime --to-revision <previous>

Testing and compliance
- Runbooks must be tested at least quarterly by the service owner; test date and result stored in the runbook header.
- Quarterly SRE audit: SRE will sample runbooks and postmortems to validate compliance with these standards.

Ownership and escalation
- Service owners retain primary responsibility for SLOs, runbooks, and capacity requests.
- SRE provides liaison support and runs quarterly reviews and capacity forecasting.
- Escalation matrix: on-call -> SRE manager -> Eng VP.

Appendix: Links and templates
- Postmortem template: /confluence/eng-sre/postmortem-template
- Capacity calculator: /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-calculator
- Runbook template: /confluence/eng-sre/runbook-template
body_plain_text: This page defines SRE standards and templates for SLOs, error budgets, capacity planning, incident review, operational tooling, and runbooks. It includes required SLOs (availability, latency), measurement recommendations, alerting thresholds and burn-rate automation, quarterly capacity planning steps, postmortem and incident review expectations, tooling requirements, and a runbook template with an example for high latency.
